new.title: Unveiling the Eigenvector 1 Sequence in BZQ Blazars. I. Mg II and Ultraviolet Fe II Emission in the UV Main Sequence
new.summary: We investigate the location of flat-spectrum radio quasars confirmed as blazars (BZQ-C), Fanaroff-Riley type II radio-loud (RL) quasars (FRII-Q), and radio non-detected quasars within the ultraviolet (UV) Eigenvector 1 (E1) plane defined by the Mg II line width (FWHM Mg II) and the UV Fe II strength (RFeUV). This represents the first systematic comparison of BZQ blazars with their proposed parent population in the UV E1 framework. To minimize selection biases, we construct statistically representative control subsamples and perform matched-subsample analyses in redshift and Mg II luminosity. Population differences are assessed using one- and two-dimensional non-parametric tests, including the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling, Mann-Whitney U, and Fasano-Franceschini statistics. We find that the three AGN populations occupy statistically distinct regions of the UV E1 plane. The dominant separation is driven by FWHM Mg II, with BZQ blazars systematically exhibiting narrower line profiles than FRII-Q quasars, while radio non-detected quasars lie between both populations. In contrast, RFeUV provides only limited discrimination between the RL subclasses, although it separates radio-loud from radio non-detected quasars at the population level. The observed ordering demonstrates that the UV E1 plane preserves the physical sequence expected from RL AGN unification. Inclination-dependent projection provides a natural first-order explanation for the Mg II line-width ordering. Additional differences in intrinsic BLR structure or accretion properties may contribute to the observed distributions, although the present analysis does not allow these effects to be separated independently from orientation.

new.title: Why High-Spin Prograde MAD States Are Not Realized for AGN in Nature: Consequences for AGN Phenomenology
new.summary: Quasar-like and other bright active galactic nuclei are typically radio quiet despite strong evidence that many host rapidly spinning black holes. In contrast, general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations show that high-spin prograde black holes in magnetically arrested disk (MAD) states produce the most powerful relativistic jets. We show that these results are not in conflict but instead correspond to physically distinct and mutually limiting evolutionary pathways. If accretion proceeds through radiatively efficient thin disks, then as the innermost stable circular orbit decreases with increasing prograde spin, radiative output and radiation pressure rise sharply, driving strong disk winds that remove the conditions required for effective jet formation. In this branch, high-spin prograde systems are therefore expected to be jet-suppressed. Alternatively, if accretion transitions to radiatively inefficient flows capable of producing MAD states, then the spin-up to near-maximal prograde rotation proceeds on timescales that exceed the age of the universe for the relevant systems, preventing the realization of the extreme high-spin prograde MAD configurations explored in GRMHD simulations. Within this framework, powerful jets need only be produced efficiently in counterrotating systems, not maximized there, preserving the time-dependent spin evolution central to the counterrotation versus corotation paradigm of Garofalo et al. (2010). We thus reconcile GRMHD results with observations and provide a unified interpretation of the radio-loud/radio-quiet dichotomy and the cosmic evolution of powerful radio sources.

new.title: Spectral evolution and secular shift of the Z source GX 340+0: an interpretation in the spreading layer paradigm
new.summary: We present a comprehensive spectral and timing study of the bright neutron star low-mass X-ray binary and Z source, GX 340+0, using broadband X-ray observations with AstroSat in 2020 and 2024, focusing on the evolution of physical parameters along the Z track and the origin of secular shifts of this track across different epochs. The spectra are consistently described by the same model, comprising blackbody emission from a spreading boundary layer near the neutron star surface, an accretion disk, and a Comptonizing corona. We observe a significant decrease in the blackbody temperature from ~1.2 keV on the horizontal branch (HB) to ~1.0 keV on the normal branch (NB), which likely contributes to the harder spectra on the HB and softer spectra on the NB. At the same time, the blackbody normalization varies substantially from ~440-860, indicating changes in the effective emitting area. Within the spreading layer framework, this evolution reflects changes in the extent of theradiating layer, while the large absolute normalization values suggest an additional contribution from the boundary layer. We also detect variations in the absorption column density, suggesting structural changes in the inner accretion disk, possibly linked to radiation driven puffing-up. The Comptonized flux shows a branch-dependent behavior, remaining relatively stable along the HB but decreasing along the NB. We interpret these results within a unified framework where the boundary layer, corona, and inner disk evolve coherently with accretion rate, explaining both the Z-track behavior and its secular shifts.

new.title: Light Shining Through the Moon: A Lunar-Occultation Helioscope for Solar Axions
new.summary: We propose a lunar-occultation helioscope in which the Moon suppresses the direct solar x-ray beam before solar axions enter the terrestrial magnetosphere, where they may reconvert into keV photons. We evaluate the conversion with a geomagnetic model combining the IGRF-14 internal contribution and the Tsyganenko T89 external magnetospheric contribution, retaining the two signed transverse components in the oscillation amplitude. As an explicit realizability test, we propagate a circular near-600-km polar orbit through the 12 August 2026 occultation. A $4'$-radius region around the solar center remains lunar occulted for about $470$ s while the sunward line of sight stays clear of the Earth; the coherent magnetic lever arm spans $69.1$--$96.4~\mathrm{T\,m}$ with $\mathcal I_{B,\mathrm{rms}}=76.9~\mathrm{T\,m}$. A B16-AGSS09 Primakoff calculation shows that this aperture contains $97.4\%$ of the 3--15 keV axion flux. For an explicitly specified NuSTAR-like detector benchmark, the propagated single-event exposure gives an expected low-mass 95\% C.L. sensitivity of $g_{a \gamma}=1.31\times10^{-10}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$. The proposal therefore establishes the plausibility of a distinct experimental channel for solar-axion searches, characterized by a lunar-defined spatial and temporal window and by a predictable geomagnetic modulation. A future detection would additionally provide directional access to the axion-emitting solar core, opening a complementary probe of the solar interior.

new.title: Making Reconnection Cooler: A relativistic resistive magnetohydrodynamics model for radiative collisionless reconnection
new.summary: Relativistic magnetic reconnection around astrophysical compact objects is a likely site for particle energization and multiwavelength emission. Kinetic theory has substantially modelled such collisionless radiative relativistic reconnection using a radiative drag force countering the acceleration of the particles. Here, we systematically derive an energy-momentum sink term in relativistic resistive magnetohydrodynamics (RRMHD), informed by kinetic theory and coupled with a charge-starved resistivity prescription which reproduces the fast reconnection rate seen in kinetic calculations, to model radiative losses. We show that our radiative loss term accurately captures important macroscopic properties -- including the temperature in the reconnection layer and the bulk motion energy distribution of the out-flowing plasma -- for inverse Compton cooling applied to two-dimensional RRMHD simulations of a reconnection layer and benchmarked to kinetic simulations. Our results hold in various cooling regimes with a one-to-one mapping to kinetic theory. Our radiative model lays a foundation for future RRMHD simulations of plasma in the relativistic radiative regime, such as in reconnection sites in a local turbulent flow or globally in the magnetospheres of black holes and neutron stars.

new.title: Photomeson-threshold origin of the TeV break in astrophysical neutrinos: Spectrum, flavor, resolved sources, and the ultrahigh-energy landscape
new.summary:
IceCube observes a break near 30 TeV in the diffuse astrophysical neutrino spectrum. We interpret it as the photomeson ($p\gamma$) threshold. Accelerated protons interact with the soft x rays of accreting black holes through the $\Delta(1232)$ resonance. One kinematic relation sets the break energy from the target field's lowest photon energy, the seed scale $\varepsilon_0$. The measured break fixes $\varepsilon_0\simeq0.13$ keV and supplies the low-energy suppression no sum of falling power laws can produce. Building on the $\Delta(1232)$ identification of Khatee Zathul, Fang, Halzen, and Hooper and the single-source-class photo-pion fit of Winter, Fiorillo, and Buson, we give closed-form relations that invert the four broken-power-law parameters to the source physics with no remaining freedom, namely, $\gamma_2=s$ and $\gamma_1=s-(\alpha_x-1)$ ($s$, $\alpha_x$ the proton and target photon indices), and $E_{m br}\propto[(1+ ar z)\varepsilon_0]^{-1}$. The break width bounds the total smearing to $\sigma_s\le0.235$ dex (68% CL), no broader than redshift alone must make it, and the seed scale is the same across sources to within a factor $\lesssim$1.5, which mean-spectrum fits do not provide. Below-break neutrinos are predicted to come on average from higher redshifts than those above. The threshold also fixes the flavor and $
u/ ar
u$ composition, including the energy-dependent $ ar
u_e$ fraction and the Glashow-resonance discriminator of Winter et al., matching current flavor data. Inverted source by source, the relation gives each resolved IceCube source its target photon scale, from the keV coronae of NGC 1068 and PKS 1424+240 to the $\sim$20 eV jet of TXS 0506+056. That two-decade spread means they cannot supply the homogeneous break, which requires a separate, fainter population. KM3-230213A points to a warm-dust target, $\varepsilon_0\simeq0.02$ eV, unless cosmogenic.

new.title: On the Sensitivity of Fermi-LAT Maximum Likelihood Stacking
new.summary: Stacking sub-threshold gamma-ray sources has become common practice for understanding high-energy emission processes at the population level. In this procedure, one co-adds log-likelihood ratios, called TS values (TS = 2ln$(L_1/L_0)$), for a source class of interest. It is best practice to compare the population of sub-threshold targets against a population of control field test sources (CFs) selected to represent the unmodeled \gray\ background. Determining the significance of a TS measurement stack has typically been difficult. In this work, we find the necessary cumulative TS value ($\Sigma$TS) of a sub-threshold population of $N$ targets to achieve a $5\sigma$ separation from a like-sized population of CFs. We find that the $\Delta (\Sigma$TS) needed to achieve a $5\sigma$ separation is $\sim 70$. In taking this measurement, we characterize the source distribution corresponding to the measured $\Sigma$TS for a significantly detected stack and even predict new individual source detections in larger stacks.

new.title: Early Evolution of Strange Quark Stars Admixed with Fermionic Dark Matter
new.summary: We study strange quark stars admixed with fermionic dark matter (DM) in three quasistatic stages of their early evolution: the neutrino-trapped stage, the heated stage after deleptonization, and the cold stage. Quark matter is described by the MIT bag model at finite temperature with thermal gluons, a repulsive vector interaction, and, in the first stage, trapped neutrinos. The DM is modeled as a cold, asymmetric gas of fermions with masses $m_\chi = 0.3$, $1$, and $3$ GeV, with and without a repulsive self-interaction, and interacts with the quark matter only through gravity. Using the two-fluid Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations, we compute the structure, the maximum masses, and the tidal deformability of the stars in each stage for DM mass fractions $F_D$ up to $5\%$, and we follow individual stars at fixed numbers of baryons and DM particles. The effect of DM is nearly the same in the three stages: for $m_\chi = 1$ GeV and $F_D = 5\%$, DM lowers the maximum mass by about $8\%$ and the tidal deformability of a $1.4\,M_\odot$ star by about $26\%$ in each stage, whereas the stage itself changes these quantities by only a few percent. Heavy DM forms a compact core; for $m_\chi = 3$ GeV without self-interaction, the mass limit of this core can set the maximum mass of the star. Light DM can form an extended halo, which does not increase the maximum mass for the fractions considered. For $m_\chi = 1$ GeV and $F_D = 5\%$, DM lowers the largest baryon mass of a newborn star by about $0.23\,M_\odot$, but this limit increases from the neutrino-trapped to the cold stage in all cases considered, so that DM does not cause a delayed collapse to a black hole. In our model, pulsars of about $2\,M_\odot$ require a stiff quark equation of state and restrict the DM fraction to a few percent unless the DM is light.

new.title: Tearing stability of pulsar equatorial current sheets
new.summary: Harris-type current sheets have been studied extensively with particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations. These local configurations generally contain no systematic magnetic-field component normal to the current sheet. Such a component develops naturally in a global pulsar magnetosphere because reconnecting field lines connect the northern and southern magnetic hemispheres. We investigate how the normal field component affects the tearing stability and dissipation of the pulsar equatorial current sheet, and we examine the consequences for the global magnetospheric configuration. We combine the tearing-stability condition for a current sheet threaded by a normal field with the electromagnetic relations imposed by the surrounding ideal force-free magnetosphere. We also formulate a dissipative equatorial boundary condition and incorporate it into a global force-free model solved with physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). For realistic Lundquist numbers the normal magnetic field can suppress the tearing instability. Preliminary solutions indicate two distinct magnetospheric configurations: a nearly ideal CKF-like state with negligible equatorial dissipation, and a strongly dissipative state resembling the solutions of Contopoulos et al. (2014) and Cerutti et al. (2015). The reconnection rate in the pulsar equatorial current sheet cannot be inferred from local Harris-type current sheet calculations because it depends on the global magnetic topology. Present global 3D PIC simulations operate at effective Lundquist numbers far below astrophysical values, and may therefore exhibit tearing that in a real pulsar magnetosphere would be strongly suppressed.

new.title: Probabilistic foreground diagnostics from dispersion measure excess in individual fast radio bursts
new.summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) provide a unique probe of diffuse baryons through their dispersion measure (DM), but interpreting a large DM for an individual burst is limited by the uncertain contribution from its host galaxy, which is hard to directly observed. We address this gap with a source-level diagnostic framework that treats $\mathrm{DM_{host}}$ as a latent variable drawn from a shared lognormal population, thereby marginalizing over the uncertain host contribution. Applying an expectation--maximization (EM) inference scheme to 92 localized FRBs, we jointly estimate the host-DM population and obtain a model-conditioned host-DM distribution for each burst. We propagate these distributions into an excess cosmological DM for each sightline, quantifying both its uncertainty and the probability that a positive excess remains after accounting for the host contribution. FRBs previously reported to show evidence for foreground or intervening contributions preferentially exhibit high probabilities of retaining such an excess, indicating that this source-level probability can provide a useful statistic for prioritizing foreground follow-up observations. Using this diagnostic, we identify 18 additional localized FRBs as high-priority candidates for follow-up searches for possible intervening galaxies, groups, clusters, or large-scale structure.

new.title: Probing Accretion Disk Dynamics of GS 1354-64: Insights from 2025$-$2026 Complex Outburst
new.summary: We present a comprehensive spectro-temporal study of the 2025--2026 outburst of the Galactic black hole X-ray binary GS 1354$-$64 using observations from MAXI/GSC, Insight-HXMT, and NuSTAR. The source underwent a $\sim126$ day outburst characterized by an `unusual' sequence of spectral states driven by three short X-ray flares ($\sim2$, 5, and 7~days), likely triggered by episodic enhancements in the Keplerian flow. These flares produced rapid spectral softening and delayed the outburst decay. The MAXI/GSC light curves show soft X-ray dominance during the intermediate $\sim90$ days of the outburst. Corresponding minima in the hardness ratio and forward-to-backward loops in the hardness--intensity diagram indicate repeated spectral softening and episodic changes in the accretion flow. Low-frequency type-C QPOs exhibit a three-phase evolution, with frequencies increasing from $0.07$ to $5.76$~Hz, decreasing from $6.14$ to $3.26$~Hz, and rising again to $6.25$~Hz with a sporadic detection of type-B QPOs in the intermediate state. The propagating oscillatory shock model successfully reproduces this evolution through inward shock propagation during the rising phase, followed by rapid outward and gradual inward motion during plateau-1, tracing changes in the Comptonizing corona. Broadband ($2-70$~keV) spectral analysis reveals coupled evolution of the thermal (diskbb: $T_{\rm in}=0.25$--$1.04$~keV) and Comptonized (thcomp: $\Gamma_{\rm th}=1.69$--$2.66$, $f_{\rm cov}\sim0.02$--$0.97$) components. Relativistic reflection is well described by the relline model, while an additional powerlaw above $\sim50$~keV in the initial hard state suggests a high-energy component, possibly associated with synchrotron cooling. Strong correlations between QPO frequency, photon index, and hardness ratio constrain the evolution of the accretion flow geometry and Comptonizing corona.

new.title: Long-Term Evolution of Hills-Captured Stars with TDE Disk Collisions: Links to Repeating Nuclear Transients
new.summary: Quasi-periodic eruptions (QPEs) and repeating partial tidal disruption event (rpTDE) candidates are widely interpreted as being powered by a star on an hours-to-years orbit around a massive black hole (MBH). Every such orbiter model presupposes a star delivered onto an extraordinarily compact orbit without being destroyed, but it is unclear whether this is achievable. We follow the coupled orbital and stellar evolution of stars captured by the Hills mechanism, combining gas drag and per-collision mass loss from recurrent TDE disks with gravitational-wave (GW) orbital decay and stochastic two-body relaxation in a Monte Carlo model. Conventionally, the EMRI-formation criterion is based on comparing the timescales of GW decay and orbital angular momentum relaxation. We find that this criterion severely overestimates the EMRI rate: for relaxation timescales shorter than a Hubble time, most Hills-captured stars are tidally disrupted before GW emission can circularize the stellar orbit. Instead, TDE-disk drag plays a crucial role in the orbital evolution and can boost the fraction of stars reaching QPE orbits by an order of magnitude or more, assuming that the disk aspect ratio is relatively large $H/r \sim 0.1$. We also find that collisional ablation imposes a minimum orbital period that rises with MBH mass and precludes sub-day orbits for $M_{\rm BH} \gtrsim 10^6\,M_\odot$, unless GWs alone can drive orbital decay faster than orbital relaxation. This can explain the observed preference of short-period QPEs for low-mass MBHs. Most known rpTDEs lie below the Hills-capture period minimum and thus require additional orbital decay, which TDE-disk drag can plausibly supply. These results support the viability of the orbiter model; our predictions of the MBH mass and orbital period distributions can be used to further test this model.

new.title: Scintillation arcs for fast pulsar binaries: the Double Pulsar
new.summary: The double pulsar PSR J0737-3039A is a prime system for tests of gravity. A precise distance would strengthen these tests and also open up the possibility to measure the fast pulsar's moment of inertia, allowing a direct constraint on the equation of state of ultra-dense matter. Current parallax estimates from pulsar timing and very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) are in tension, which motivates complementary constraints. Information about distances is encoded in pulsar scintillation, but a complication for the double pulsar is that rapid orbital motion makes the interpretation difficult. We introduce an orbital motion ``resampling'' technique to overcome this complication, and use it to determine the properties of the principal scattering screen and the pulsar binary. Our fits yield a pulsar distance, of $781^{+62}_{-94}{\rm\,pc}$, in better agreement with the VLBI-based distance, but find that the nearly edge-on orbit precludes a precise measurement. For the principal screen, we infer a distance of $270^{+24}_{-23}{\rm\,pc}$, an orientation of $73.1^{\circ}\pm2.6^{\circ}$ E of N, and a transverse speed of $-15.2\pm1.0{\rm\,km/s}$. We also demonstrate the presence of a second screen, whose properties we can only partially determine: it is oriented roughly perpendicularly to the first screen and at a larger distance, of $\gtrsim\!547{\rm\,pc}$. To benchmark our technique and its uncertainties, we develop simulations of the system, generating artificial data that match the characteristics of the observed ones. We also discuss how future improvements to the method and use of the second screen could enable a more precise distance measurement.

figures.caption: Sketch of the geometry. The left-most plane shows the motion of pulsar A on the sky, at a distance d p d_{p} , as seen from the solar system barycenter, with its trajectory during an observation shown as the solid line. Radiation from the pulsar can follow multiple paths to reach the observer: directly, via the line of sight, indicated by the black line, and indirectly, scattered by one or more scattering screens, with examples of single-scattered rays shown with the yellow and blue lines. The two middle planes each represent a scattering screen, at distance d s d_{s} . The scattering is assumed to be due to highly anisotropic density gradients, indicated by the bands, so that light can be bent in only one direction. This results in sets of scattering points which are on a line perpendicular to the bands, at orientation ξ \xi , and which may move with velocity v s v_{s} along that direction (the other direction is not measurable). The right-most plane shows the motion of the Earth around the Sun, as projected on the plane perpendicular to the line of sight. The latin numerals mark four times, for each of which a panel in the bottom shows the effective pulsar position, as projected on each of the two screens. One sees that the amplitude of the projected orbital motion is similar for the two screens: while screen 2 is closer to the pulsar than screen 1, which leads to larger projected motion, it is also less aligned, which reduces it. The annual variation, however, is much larger for the first screen, because Earth’s motion is aligned much better with it.

figures.caption: Arc curvature measurements made in Doppler-delay spectra for different observations. The black solid lines indicate the lowest and highest valid curvature, as estimated by eye, while the red line shows the curvature expected from our fit to all data. In estimating the curvature, the difficulty is that what one observes is an auto-correlation of an underlying wavefield. Hence, if near the bottom of the main arc, where there is most power, the arc is asymmetric to one side, in the arclets across the arc the power will distributed preferentially to the other side. Top: Sample S-band observation, with a clearly defined, simple arc, with the power at the bottom fairly symmetric. Middle: Sample L-band observation, with clearer evidence for asymmetry near the base, and thus opposite asymmetry in the arclets. If one were to fit a parabola directly, one would infer the wrong curvature (or an offset from the origin). Bottom: Sample UHF-band observation, with again clear evidence for asymmetry.

new.title: Dual Horizon-MAD: A New Mode of Binary Black Hole Magnetically Arrested Accretion with Saturated Horizon Magnetic Fluxes and Intermittent Minidisks
new.summary: Reliable first-principles predictions of multimessenger signals from inspiralling supermassive binary black holes (SMBBHs) require magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations in full general relativity (GR) that resolve the accretion flow down to the black hole horizons. However, performing such simulations long enough to relax the magnetohydrodynamics near the BBHs is computationally challenging and a source of uncertainty in modeling efforts. In this work, we present the longest MHD simulation of circumbinary disk (CBD) accretion onto a SMBBH in full GR. The equal-mass, quasicircular, nonspining BBH starts at an initial separation of $d/M=30$ and evolves over $\sim56$ orbits ($t \simeq 52,000 \, GM/c^3$), relaxing the magnetic field dynamics within the CBD cavity. After $\sim 23$ orbits and persistent magnetically arrested minidisks, the accretion enters a new magnetically arrested mode which we call dual horizon-MAD (DH-MAD). In DH-MAD, the dimensionless horizon magnetic fluxes remain saturated at $\phi_{BH}\sim 20$ driving magnetic flux eruptions from the vicinity of the BH horizons, and the vertical magnetic flux in the cavity saturates, but no flux eruptions occur at the cavity-CBD boundary. During this DH-MAD phase, there is also a shift in the total mass accretion rate variability, which exhibits a periodicity of $f\sim 1.8 f_{\rm orb}$, while the accretion rate modulation on the individual black holes occurs almost at the orbital period, $f\sim 0.9 f_{\rm orb}$. $\phi_{BH}$ also exhibits a robust periodicity at $f\sim 0.4 f_{\rm orb}$, suggesting that quasiperiodic nonthermal emission from magnetic reconnection near the horizons could be a smoking gun electromagnetic counterpart to inspiraling SMBBHs. Finally, minidisks around the BHs become intermittent in the DH-MAD phase, even at a separation of $d/M = 24$, likely due to the large plasma magnetization in the optically thin cavity.

new.title: Fast Radio Bursts Co-detected by CHIME/FRB and DSA-110 from 400 to 1530 MHz
new.summary: We present a sample of $15$ fast radio bursts (FRBs) that were co-detected by the Deep Synoptic Array (DSA-110) and the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) between 2022 and 2024, of which $12$ have channelized voltage data from both instruments and 9 have secure redshifts. All but one are as-yet-non-repeating. Most bursts span the entire bandwidth of each instrument (400-800 MHz for CHIME, 1280-1530 MHz for DSA-110), significantly expanding the number of FRBs known to emit across $>1$ GHz of spectral bandwidth and constraining the spectral evolution of energy and propagation effects. On average, the FRBs exhibit higher spectral energies (up to a factor of $\sim10$) in the CHIME band but are lower in peak flux density due to substantial pulse broadening. The sample mean (median) spectral index $-0.4\pm0.4$ ($-0.3\pm0.4$) is shallower than previously reported spectral indices, likely a selection effect. A third of the sample shows evidence for a spectral turnover, comparable to that seen in GHz-peaked pulsar and magnetar spectra. Joint scintillation and pulse broadening constraints indicate that nearly all bursts encounter multiple scattering screens, with pulse broadening originating within their host galaxies. The co-detected bursts are among the most scattered in the CHIME/FRB sample, while being the narrowest in the DSA-110 sample, indicating that CHIME/FRB and DSA-110 select different subsets of the FRB population; the interplay between intrinsic burst width, scattering, and the FRB search time resolution creates a narrow window of sensitivity to co-detected FRBs, providing a blueprint for future ultra-wideband FRB surveys.

new.title: Spectropolarimetric properties of fast radio bursts co-detected by CHIME/FRB and DSA-110
new.summary: We present spectropolarimetric analysis of twelve fast radio bursts (FRBs) co-detected by CHIME/FRB and DSA-110, eleven of which are apparently non-repeating. We obtain broadband spectral coverage (400-1530 MHz) for these FRBs and constrain propagation effects in their polarized spectra. We observe two notable spectral features: (i) in three FRBs, we find decreasing linear polarization fraction with increasing frequency and, (ii) in seven FRBs, we find that the linear polarization fraction decreases with decreasing frequency. The former spectral signature is commonly observed in radio pulsars and is suggestive of magnetospheric emission, where either the mixing of orthogonally polarized modes or incoherent summing of unresolved burst components may cause depolarization at high frequencies. The latter is consistent with depolarization due to multipath propagation. We report the first statistically significant correlation (3.5-3.9$\sigma$) between the extent of depolarization and amplitude of Faraday rotation arising from FRB host galaxies, implying that the two effects likely arise in the same turbulent, magnetoionic environments around FRB sources. The prevalence of depolarization in our sample suggests that turbulent environments that have, thus far, been predominantly associated with some repeating FRBs, may also be commonly present around a subset of apparently non-repeating FRBs. We highlight a systematic bias for detecting a disproportionately high fraction of constant polarization angle (PA) profiles in low-frequency FRB surveys due to amplified scatter broadening, which we also observe in two of our co-detected FRBs.

new.title: The FRB Population Revisited: Rate, Energy, Evolution, and Host-DM Constraints from the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog
new.summary: We present a study that simultaneously fits for key fast radio burst (FRB) population properties using the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog while calibrating for instrumental selection effects. Our inferred volumetric rate at $z=0$ is $1.1^{+0.4}_{-0.3}\times 10^{5}\,{\rm Gpc}^{-3}\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ above an isotropic-equivalent energy of $10^{39}$ erg and below a scattering timescale of 30 ms at 600 MHz. The evolution of the FRB rate relative to the cosmic star formation rate remains statistically unconstrained. Assuming a Schechter function for the energy distribution, isotropic emission, and 1-GHz emission bandwidth, we find a characteristic maximum energy of $2.0^{+2.6}_{-1.0} \times 10^{41}$ erg and a differential power-law index of $-1.41\,^{+0.27}_{-0.21}({\rm stat.})\,\pm\,0.35({\rm sys.})$. The host galaxy contribution to the observed dispersion measure (DM) is modeled as a log-normal distribution; assuming a total Galactic contribution of 80 $\text{pc cm}^{-3}$, we find a median host-galaxy DM contribution of $199^{+34}_{-36}\;\text{pc cm}^{-3}$ in the rest-frame. Finally, we find that the average FRB spectrum, described by a spectral index of $\alpha=-1.0^{+0.5}_{-0.6}$, is inconsistent with being flat at the $\sim2\sigma$ level. We note an excess of high-S/N bursts at low DMs in the observed sample that is not predicted by the best-fit model. Testing alternative models does not alleviate this tension; future population studies may mitigate this limitation by incorporating robust fluence and redshift measurements.

new.title: The Most X-ray Luminous Fast Blue Optical Transient at Early Times: AT 2024qfm and Inefficient Reprocessing of Its High-Energy Emission
new.summary: We present comprehensive multiwavelength (X-ray, UV, optical, and radio) observations of the Luminous Fast Blue Optical Transient (LFBOT) AT 2024qfm. At $z = 0.227$ and reaching $L_{\rm x}\approx 10^{44}\,\rm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, AT 2024qfm is the most X-ray luminous LFBOT at $\delta t < 20$ days, and the least luminous at mm wavelengths. The X-ray emission shows a rapid ($\propto t^{-6}$) decay in the first $\approx 6$ days followed by a brightening at $\delta t \approx 15$ days that is accompanied by significant spectral hardening. Similarly to other LFBOTs, optical spectra remain featureless, and the UV-optical emission is dominated by a hot thermal continuum with temperature $T> 10000$ K until $\delta t \approx 14$ days. AT 2024qfm shows luminous radio emission that is broadly consistent with the interaction of a fast ($\Gamma \beta c \approx 0.2$ c) shock wave with a dense medium ($n_{\rm CSM} \approx 6 \times 10^{4}\, \rm cm^{-3}$ at $R \approx 1.3 \times 10^{16}$ cm). Interestingly, the radio spectra do not evolve between $\delta t \approx 40-58$ days, indicating multiple outflow components shocking the surrounding medium. Peculiar to AT2024qfm is that this LFBOT reaches $L_{\rm x} \approx L_{\rm opt}$ at much earlier times ($\delta t \approx 7$ days) than observed for AT 2018cow and AT 2024wpp, suggesting less efficient re-processing of X-rays. Finally, a compilation of the X-ray spectral properties of all known LFBOTs shows that they consistently exhibit harder X-ray spectra than GRB afterglows, indicating a different emission mechanism and/or regimes between the two source classes.

new.title: Sound of Keplerian binaries in a homogeneous Newtonian fluid background
new.summary: We formulate the dissipation due to sound-wave emission from a Keplerian binary embedded in a homogeneous Newtonian fluid background at rest in the binary center-of-mass frame within linear perturbation theory. Rather than starting from the local wake force, we treat the binary as a localized periodic mass source and compute the sound-wave fluxes carried away by the medium. The time-averaged energy, linear-momentum, and angular-momentum fluxes are obtained from Noether currents of the fluid perturbations. For a classical inviscid barotropic Newtonian fluid, retaining the self-gravity of density perturbations while adopting the Jeans prescription, we derive explicit flux formulas for circular and eccentric binaries with arbitrary mass ratio. This formulation also clarifies the ultraviolet behavior of point sources: in a nondispersive fluid, the harmonic sum becomes cutoff-sensitive precisely when at least one component becomes supersonic. We examine explicitly how finite source size removes this divergence using a uniform-sphere model and relate the resulting regularization to a corresponding effective harmonic cutoff. The associated secular eccentricity evolution exhibits circularization in the subsonic regime when the fluid self-gravity is sufficiently weak but can change sign outside this regime, with eccentricity growth in the strictly supersonic UV limit. For a Schrödinger-Poisson quantum fluid, quantum pressure instead softens the high-frequency contribution and renders the point-source fluxes UV finite within the nonrelativistic regime; our numerical results further indicate eccentricity growth due to sound radiation over the parameter space explored. Finally, we translate orbital-decay measurements of two binary pulsars into order-of-magnitude bounds on the homogeneous quantum-fluid density surrounding each system.

new.title: Is the learner or the summary the limit? Auditing machine-learning energy reconstruction for air-shower arrays on KASCADE and GRAPES-3
new.summary: Machine-learning energy estimators for cosmic-ray arrays are usually trained on a few fitted shower parameters, not station signals. When their resolution stops improving, standard diagnostics cannot say whether a better model would help or the summary has run out of information. We use a five-step audit that compares trained models with a learner-independent estimate of the lowest error the summary allows (its squared-loss Bayes risk, or floor), tests which inputs add information and flags inputs merely computed from the fit. We apply it to public KASCADE simulations with three hadronic-interaction models (QGSJET-II-04, EPOS-LHC and SIBYLL-2.3d), to 13,848,509 measured KASCADE events and to simulated GRAPES-3 events. Within known energy decades below 10^16 eV, gradient boosting on nine reconstructed features is within 2.2% of the estimated floor under every estimator setting, so more capacity is not expected to gain more than about 2%. The floor is an estimate, accurate to about 1% in a semi-synthetic benchmark with intervals that under-cover, and not a bound on the true Bayes risk. Replacing reconstructed by true particle numbers removes 70 to 72% of the error variance below 10^15 eV and 24 to 26% between 10^16 and 10^17 eV on all three models, yet simulated station signals close about a tenth of that gap. On GRAPES-3, networks given images rendered from the fit do no better than the fit. In measured data, the mean muon size at fixed electron size lies within every model's proton-to-iron bracket and a label-free probe finds the muon channel used as in simulation; neither fixes the energy scale. Energy-labelled results are simulated.

new.title: On extracting Science information from a large data set of RXTE X-ray binary spectra using KDE technique
new.summary: Machine Learning/Neural Networks have been successively and extensively used in Astronomy (and other subjects) for class identification of objects based on large data sets. However, it remains difficult to extract other science information, such as what the characteristics of the class are that allow for definite identification, and whether there are objects in the sample that are unique and hence of possible science interest. An alternate approach based on rank ordering of variables and Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) may be used for class identification and to infer such science information. We test the method on a previously analyzed data set of RXTE spectra of low-mass X-ray binaries and find that black hole and neutron star systems can be distinguished at an accuracy level of ~93%, which is comparable to deep learning techniques. The soft state spectra of black hole systems are distinct from neutron star ones. For the whole sample, observations of the pulsar 4U 1907+097 (which was inadvertently introduced into the data set) were clearly found to be unique. The previously reported hyper-soft states of GRO J1655-40 and XTE J1550-564 are found to be unique among black hole spectra. For the rest of the neutron stars, the method identifies some unreported spectra of EXO 1745-248 as unique because they seem to be relativistic reflection-dominated spectra. We discuss the potential and scalability of this method.

new.title: Survey of Compact Sources for Pulsars and Exotic Objects-II. Precision Timing of Millisecond Pulsar J1840+1102
new.summary: We present the timing analysis of the eclipsing millisecond pulsar PSR J1840+1102, discovered in the Survey of COmpact sources for Pulsars and Exotic objects (SCOPE) using the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT). PSR J1840+1102 has a short spin period of 1.60 ms and an orbital period of 1.68 days, with a dispersion measure (DM) of 98.8 pc cm$^{-3}$. We report timing analysis over a 2.7-year baseline, yielding a phase-connected solution with a post-fit residual RMS of 2.1 $\mu$s. Enabled by the timing solution, we report discovery of pulsed gamma-rays from PSR J1840+1102, with the gamma-ray peak aligned with that of the radio profile. PSR J1840+1102 also exhibits remarkably short eclipses, lasting only around $0.4\%$ of the total orbit at 650 MHz. Based on optical searches, the orbital parameters, short eclipses, and comparison with the known binary pulsar population, we infer a Helium white dwarf (He-WD) surrounded by plasma to be the most likely companion. Furthermore, using GMRT observations covering 300 to 750 MHz, we present a study of the interstellar medium properties towards PSR J1840+1102 including refractive scintillation, DM variations and scattering, and report a very low scattering index of $1.65\pm0.15$. The low timing residuals and lack of any prominent orbital parameters or DM variations support the overall suitability of PSR J1840+1102 for inclusion in the pulsar timing array campaigns.

new.title: Finite-temperature quark dynamics in proto-neutron stars: Maximum baryonic mass and radial oscillations
new.summary: Finite-temperature quark dynamics can significantly alter proto-neutron star evolution even when the cold equation of state remains unchanged. We quantify this sensitivity by comparing a purely hadronic baseline with two hybrid models incorporating quark matter via the Polyakov-Nambu-Jona-Lasinio (PNJL) framework and its entanglement extension (EPNJL), which isolates the role of finite-temperature chiral-deconfinement coupling. Employing bulk Gibbs constructions for both nuclear liquid-gas and hadron-quark phase coexistence, we compute equilibrium configurations across hot neutrino-trapped, hot neutrino-free, and cold stages, alongside linear radial oscillations of selected hot neutrino-free stars. Introducing quarks lowers the maximum baryonic mass at every stage and reverses its evolutionary ordering: whereas the maximum baryonic mass increases toward the cold limit in the purely hadronic model, it decreases progressively in both hybrid models, opening mass windows for delayed collapse. Crucially, despite sharing the same cold limit, PNJL and EPNJL yield distinct baryonic-mass intervals for mixed-core survival across stages: only EPNJL permits configurations that retain mixed cores across both hot stages, whereas only PNJL allows hot neutrino-free mixed-core stars to possess cold equilibrium counterparts. All tested hot neutrino-free mixed-core stars remain linearly stable, yet their fundamental radial frequencies differ substantially. These findings demonstrate that finite-temperature quark dynamics imprints distinct evolutionary constraints and pulsation signatures on proto-neutron stars beyond cold-matter descriptions.

new.title: Reliability of Fermi/GBM spectral-catalogue parameters for gamma-ray burst population studies
new.summary: The Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (GBM) spectral catalogue contains measurements affected by model uncertainties, different peak-flux (PFLX) integration times, and changes in catalogue processing. We examine which quantities describe spectral shape and which reflect brightness or measurement conditions. We analysed 3337 of 3378 GRBs with spectral-fit data and identified a catalogue transition at GRB180712358. We compared the two periods using rank-based tests, regressions, and catalogue model-selection rules, and assessed duration classification by repeated cross-validation. PFLX measurements at 64 and nominal 1024 ms were analysed separately; short-long comparisons used fluence (FLNC) measurements only. The transition coincides with changes in catalogue version, fit statistic, and fit fields. In the nominal 1024 ms sample, all ten COMP A-B rank-biserial effects have absolute values below 0.10. In the 64 ms sample, COMP shape parameters are similar, but amplitudes, fluxes, and fluences are higher in the later period. The origin of this difference is unknown. In the earlier period, brighter bursts have smaller parameter errors but larger reported fit statistics and stronger evidence for spectral curvature. The FLNC PLAW index measures broad-band hardness. BAND alpha and Epeak can describe spectral shape when their errors are controlled, but beta is often poorly constrained. Adding PLAW or BAND to COMP provides little additional duration-classification information in matched samples. We interpret the A-B division mainly as a catalogue-processing transition, not population evolution. Fit statistics, errors, metadata, and model labels describe measurement conditions and should not be treated as independent physical variables. Correlated model parameters should not be treated as independent.

new.title: A Positron Spectral Dip near 20 GV in Selected Orbital Projections of AMS-02 Data
new.summary: We analyze more than a decade of public Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS-02) data (2011-2021), matching daily electron and positron spectra to the orbital record on 3268 common dates. For each sky window we weight the spectra by the time the orbital zenith spends there and divide each rigidity bin by its all-date mean. At 16.6-22.8 GV, the normalized positron flux dips below its neighboring bins in several projections. At the Galactic center and the Crab, the positron dip exceeds the electron dip by $3.04\pm1.19$ and $3.57\pm1.22$ percentage points, respectively (statistical errors). A scan centered on 1177 Fermi-LAT catalog sources also finds dips at PKS~0301$-$243 and PKS~1424+240. At fixed rigidity, 13.8\% of trials that shift the spectra relative to the orbit produce a dip somewhere in the catalog at least as deep as the observed maximum. An isotropic intensity with the measured daily spectra reproduces every projection exactly. In a zenith pencil-beam model, direct positron annihilation on a common cold-electron column at the Galactic center and the Crab produces less than 0.10 percentage points of dip depth in either projection.

new.title: The XRISM view of the front and rear ejecta dynamics in Tycho's SNR
new.summary: We present a line-of-sight dynamics study of Tycho's supernova remnant (SNR) with XRISM/Resolve, based on five pointings obtained during the first two years of the mission. Thanks to a spectral resolution better than 5 eV, the spectra reveal a clear Doppler splitting of the Si, S, Ar, Ca and Fe emission lines towards the center of the remnant, allowing us to study the front and back sides of the shocked ejecta independently for the first time. Using a phenomenological Gaussian line model and a Bayesian fitting method, we analyze the broadband spectra of each pointing and of 149 individual pixels. We derive the dynamics and flux of the front and back sides for each element, as well as a global line broadening. The dynamics of Tycho's SNR are asymmetric, with the back side expanding faster than the front side for Si, S and Fe. We reveal a line-of-sight stratification of the elements, with Fe at lower velocities than Si and S. Si shows a strong front/back flux asymmetry, the front side being up to twice as bright as the back side in the northeastern part of the remnant. A similar but weaker asymmetry is found for S. For Fe, the flux ratio varies spatially, with either side dominating. These measurements allow us to reassess the average line-of-sight kinematics obtained at CCD resolution, which is affected by the flux asymmetry between the front and back sides and not only by a velocity asymmetry. Combining our line-of-sight velocities with Chandra proper motions, we reconstruct the three-dimensional dynamics of Tycho's SNR. Finally, we discuss the constraints these results set on the explosion model and the progenitor system.

new.title: Detection of a warm absorber in a highly variable low-redshift quasar
new.summary: { 3XMMJ115535.8+232723 (z=0.136) is a low-redshift radio-quiet quasar, which shows an unusual spectral nature. The X-ray properties and variability of this source have never been studied.} {Using numerous X-ray observations, this study aims to perform a detailed spectral analysis for 3XMMJ115535.8+232723. Having produced spectra from different flux states, the aims of the study is to investigate long-term spectral behaviour in a single object outside the local group of AGNs.} { We used {\it XMM-Newton} and {\it Chandra} observations of quasar 3XMMJ115535.8+232723 obtained between 2000 and 2008 to derive the spectroscopic details. We analyzed 0.3--10 keV spectra using an absorbed powerlaw model in combination with a warm absorber component.} {The first spectroscopic analysis of 3XMMJ115535.8+232723 reveals that the X-ray spectrum imprints a strong absorption feature, prominent at $\sim 0.7$ keV, which has been interpreted to be due to absorption in a partially ionized material (a.k.a. warm absorber). The column density and ionization parameter of the warm absorber vary by more than an order of magnitude for different observations. The results are consistent with high density clouds located ($\sim 1000$ gravitational radius) from the central region and another set of low density clouds further away. The intrinsic flux and spectral shape of the source also varies significantly over the observations.}

new.title: XRISM view of a featureless cluster Abell 1060: Revealing the advection of a diffuse radio source by ICM motions
new.summary: Abell 1060 is a nearby, dynamically relaxed galaxy cluster hosting the extended radio structure Flying Fox (FF) near its center. We used high-resolution XRISM/Resolve spectroscopy to measure intracluster medium (ICM) motions and velocity dispersion. Spatially resolved analysis reveals a velocity gradient of approximately 100 km/s along FF and enhanced velocity dispersion near the brightest cluster galaxy NGC 3311, suggesting turbulence generated by galaxy-ICM interactions. These results and the compact extent of FF favor fossil plasma supplied by past activity of the brightest cluster galaxy and transported by ICM motions. We also tested whether the measured turbulence could generate or maintain the nonthermal components of FF. For a velocity dispersion of $96.7^{+23.9}_{-24.6}$ km/s and an assumed turbulence scale of 50 kpc, comparable to the Resolve field of view and approximately half the cluster core radius, the turbulent energy flux is approximately $3.49 \times 10^{-28}$ erg cm$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$. Although this flux may weakly reenergize pre-existing relativistic electrons, the acceleration timescale of approximately 2.5 Gyr exceeds the synchrotron and inverse Compton cooling timescale of approximately 210 Myr. The present turbulence is therefore insufficient to accelerate electrons to high energies. In situ turbulent reacceleration is unlikely to dominate the generation of FF, although it may help maintain fossil electrons supplied by past AGN activity. These results link ICM dynamics to the origin of nonthermal emission and support a time-evolutionary picture of particle acceleration in galaxy clusters.

new.title: Radiation-Hydrodynamical Modeling of Accretion Columns in Ultraluminous X-ray Pulsars
new.summary: Ultraluminous X-ray pulsars (ULXPs) provide a unique laboratory for studying accretion-column physics under strongly magnetized super-Eddington conditions. In this work, we employ a one-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamical model to investigate the vertical structure of ULXP accretion columns, applying it to NGC 300 ULX-1, Swift J0243.6$+$6124, and SMC X-3. We solve the coupled conservation equations for the inflowing gas and radiation field in a dipole-funnel geometry, allowing the velocity, density, gas pressure, radiation pressure, total energy transport rate, radiation sonic surface, and thermal mound location to be determined self-consistently. We find that radiation pressure naturally produces an extended sinking region above the stellar surface, where the inflowing gas is gradually decelerated and its kinetic energy is converted into radiation energy that partly escapes through the column walls. Despite their different luminosities, magnetic fields, and column geometries, the radiation sonic surfaces are tightly clustered near $15$ km, indicating a similar large-scale radiative deceleration structure. These results show that ULXP accretion columns develop extended radiation-dominated structures regulated by the mass accretion rate, magnetic scattering opacity, and column geometry. The dynamical profiles obtained here provide a physical basis for interpreting radiation-dominated accretion columns in ULXPs and for future physics-based spectral modeling.

new.title: Interpreting the $γ$-Ray Emission of the Cygnus X region with a Combined Cygnus OB2 and Cygnus X-3 Scenario
new.summary: The recent detection of high-energy $\gamma$-ray emission up to PeV energies from the Cygnus X region points to the presence of a PeVatron therein. This region hosts notable candidates such as the Cygnus OB2 association, which may be associated with PeV $\gamma$-photons detected by the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO). The X-ray binary Cygnus X-3 also lies along the line of sight to the Cygnus X region, and LHAASO has observed modulated PeV $\gamma$-ray flux from its direction, indicating that its contribution is also non-negligible. Here, we attempt to interpret the $\gamma$-ray emission of the Cygnus X region using a combined scenario. Assuming a hadronic origin, we consider contributions from Cygnus OB2, Cygnus X-3, and Galactic cosmic rays (GCRs). Our results show that Cygnus OB2 alone, or its combination with the GCR component, is insufficient to account for the multiwavelength observations, whereas including the $\gamma$-ray emission from Cygnus X-3 naturally explains these observations. This suggests that the $\gamma$-ray emission from the Cygnus X region has a more complex origin, necessitating a joint consideration of Cygnus OB2 and Cygnus X-3. The expected neutrino flux from hadronic interactions extends into the GeV band and can help reveal the radiation mechanism of Cygnus X-3, underscoring the need for high-sensitivity GeV neutrino observatories.

new.title: Non-Equilibrium Steady States in Nucleosynthesis
new.summary: Steady-state behavior underlies many nucleosynthesis processes in which the population number of nuclei can remain nearly constant despite the rapid nuclear reactions. While existing theoretical descriptions largely focus on established chemical equilibrium, as in nuclear statistical equilibrium (NSE) and quasi equilibrium (QSE), non-equilibrium steady states (NESSs) can form in process-specific approximations such as classical $\beta$-flow $r$-process. We develop a general framework for describing NESSs in nuclear reaction networks by formulating the steady-state condition as a balance of reaction flows within a reduced linear description of the relevant network subset. We apply the framework to four representative nucleosynthesis scenarios spanning different steady-state regimes: disequilibrium between nucleons and $\alpha$ particles during $\alpha$-rich freeze-out, the classical $\beta$-flow steady state, the neutrino-assisted $\nu r$-process, and the fission-cycling phase of the $r$-process. In particular, the fission-cycling scenario is described by a quasi-steady-state (QSS) approximation maintaining the population ratios between two nuclei while not conserving the total number of nuclei. The framework reproduces the characteristic abundance pattern for each case while providing a unified interpretation of the underlying steady-state behavior. The eigenvalue spectrum reveals network structure and characterizes the relaxation timescales of abundance distributions. These results establish a general approach for analyzing nucleosynthesis beyond the condition of chemical equilibrium and provide a foundation for extending graph-based methods to complicated nuclear reaction networks.

new.title: Luminosity function of millisecond pulsars in globular clusters from their gamma-ray emission
new.summary: Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) are widely believed to be responsible for the gamma-ray emission of globular clusters (GCs), yet the underlying MSP gamma-ray luminosity function remains uncertain. Existing GC-based determinations of the latter often rely on external prescriptions for the number of MSPs in each cluster. In this work, we constrain the MSP gamma-ray luminosity function in Milky-Way GCs directly from gamma-ray spectral energy distributions (SEDs), establishing an inference strategy that remains computationally viable for joint analyses of large GC samples. We construct a forward model in which each GC hosts a population of MSPs whose luminosities are drawn from a universal log-normal luminosity function. Synthetic GC SEDs are generated by summing individual MSP spectra, and we infer posterior distributions using first a likelihood-based nested sampling method and then a simulation-based inference (SBI) approach. We show how the likelihood-based method becomes rapidly impractical as the number of jointly modelled clusters (and cluster-specific latent parameters) increases, whereas the SBI approach scales mildly with sample size and reproduces the likelihood-based posteriors in regimes where direct sampling is feasible. We then apply the SBI pipeline to Fermi-LAT SEDs from the 4FGL-DR4 catalog for a sample of 36 GC-associated sources, augmented by dedicated phase-resolved ON/OFF SEDs for two clusters hosting individually detected MSPs. For the real data sample, we obtain informative constraints on the luminosity-function parameters consistent with previous analyses that constrain the cluster-specific MSP counts via complementary multi-wavelength information.

new.title: Tidal effects of bulk viscosity in neutron stars
new.summary: Bulk viscosity in neutron-star matter provides a temperature-dependent mechanism for tidal dissipation. In this study, we investigate the impact of bulk viscosity on the dissipative tidal response of neutron stars composed of neutrons, protons, and electrons. Employing cold equations of state derived through the momentum-dependent interaction model, we examine the bulk viscosity arising from the direct Urca process, which acts to restore chemical equilibrium. The temperature dependence is incorporated through the weak-interaction rate, allowing us to explore the behavior of bulk viscosity in the neutrino-transparent regime at temperatures up to a few MeV. To account for the spatial distribution of bulk viscosity within neutron stars, we introduce the effective bulk viscosity, a volume-averaged quantity over the region where direct Urca process operates, and establish a connection with the bulk viscosity. Specifically, we investigate its implications for tidal quantities, including the lag time and dissipative deformability, highlighting their dependence on temperature and stellar compactness. We find that the dissipative tidal effects become maximal at a temperature approximately coinciding with the one of maximum bulk viscosity on the onset of direct Urca. Additionally, these effects are more pronounced in intermediate neutron star masses compared to maximum ones. Finally, for both canonical $1.4\;M_\odot$ and maximum-mass neutron star configurations, we derive causality-based upper bounds on these quantities, providing theoretical benchmarks for assessing the potential observability of bulk-viscous effects in gravitational-wave signals from binary neutron star inspirals.

new.title: Two-Component Model for the Unidentified Extended Fermi-LAT Source 4FGL J1908.6+0915e / FL16Y J1908.6+0915e in the SGR 1900+14--W49A Sky Region
new.summary: Galactic PeVatrons are expected to be powerful sources of non-thermal high-energy (HE, $E>100$ MeV) and very-high-energy (VHE, $E>100$ GeV) $\gamma$-ray emission as a manifestation of acceleration processes in supernova remnants (SNRs), star formation regions (SFRs), and pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe). In the sky region containing the magnetar SGR 1900+14 and the young massive star cluster (YMSC) W49A, there is one recently identified point-like source FL16Y J1910.2+0903, and there are three unidentified gamma-ray sources: the Fermi-LAT extended source FL16Y J1908.6+0915e, the HAWC extended source 4HWC J1908+0845, and the LHAASO point-like source LHAASO J1907+0913. We investigate the possibility of explaining the HE and VHE $\gamma$-ray emission from the SGR 1900+14--W49A sky region using a model of the Fermi-LAT extended source FL16Y J1908.6+0915e as superposition of two extended sources -- a potential SNR/PWN associated with the magnetar SGR 1900+14 and the stellar-wind superbubble adjacent to the YMSC W49A complex. To this end, we simulate the observed $\gamma$-ray emission in hadronic and leptonic models using the open NAIMA code and show that it consists of two extended regions: the stellar wind superbubble in W49A region -- an analog of the Westerlund 1 superbubble -- powered by the YMSC W49A (the southern part of the extended source FL16Y J1908.6+0915e); and the SGR 1900+14 region, powered by a potential SNR/PWN associated with the magnetar (the northern part of the extended source FL16Y J1908.6+0915e). However, due to the considerable distance to the magnetar ($d=12.5$ kpc), the required cosmic-ray energy budget in both hadronic and leptonic scenarios corresponds to a hypernova explosion and/or a powerful magnetar wind nebula created by a newly born millisecond magnetar with a rotational energy of the order of $10^{52}$ erg.

new.title: A Log-Normal Timing Likelihood for Direction Reconstruction of Ultra-High-Energy Gamma-Ray Air Showers
new.summary: Ultra-high-energy $\gamma$-ray observations provide a direct probe of Galactic PeVatrons. Extending measurements to multi-PeV energies requires characterizing extensive air showers over large lateral distances, where the arrival-time distribution of secondary particles becomes broad and strongly asymmetric. Conventional direction reconstruction methods approximate the shower front as a deterministic surface and minimize a $\chi^2$ function of timing residuals. Because this implicitly assumes symmetric Gaussian errors, far-axis timing information is poorly utilized. \textsc{CORSIKA} simulations show that the arrival-time distribution of $\gamma$-induced secondary particles in the shower plane at a given lateral distance is positively skewed and closely follows a log-normal function. Using this property, we develop a likelihood-based direction reconstruction method that directly models the empirical arrival-time distribution and its radial dependence while accounting for multiple particles triggering the same detector unit. Applied to simulated $\gamma$-induced air showers, the log-normal likelihood consistently improves angular resolution compared with conical and parabolic wavefront fits, with the largest relative gains for high-energy events spanning wide lateral extents. We also show that independent readout of individual detector units yields better angular resolution than merging their signals into a single station-level measurement.

new.title: X-ray polarimetry of a magnetar in the aftermath of an anti-glitch: Revisiting 1E 2259+586 with IXPE
new.summary: Magnetars display timing anomalies such as glitches and anti-glitches. 1E 2259+586, whose properties in the X-ray band were recently investigated through a joint XMM/IXPE observation campaign, has been observed to have multiple glitches and three anti-glitches, the most recent occurring in May 2025. Although the X-ray emission is currently decaying, the flux, which roughly doubled at the onset of the anti-glitch, had not yet returned to its original level at the time of the IXPE observation, and the pulse profile has also shown significant evolution. We present an analysis of the recent IXPE observation of 1E 2259+586 from late April to early May 2026. We compare the post-anti-glitch polarisation results with those obtained from the previous IXPE observation in 2023. This provides an unprecedented opportunity to monitor the spectro-polarimetric evolution of a magnetar in the wake of a hallmark event such as an anti-glitch. A dedicated 400ks IXPE DDT observation was approved to track possible changes in the polarisation with respect to the pre-anti-glitch campaign. Spectral and polarimetric properties were jointly modelled within the xspec and ixpeobssim suites, and the analysis was further expanded using a maximum-likelihood technique. No significant detection was found in the phase-averaged and energy-integrated spectrum of this observation. However, despite the significantly shorter exposure, polarisation was clearly detected in the phase-resolved spectrum and the degree of polarisation was found to have a higher best-fitting value, though still statistically consistent, than the previous measurement from 2023, reaching a level >30% in correspondence to the pulse profile minimum. In spite of some slight differences between the two observations, the polarisation trends remain largely consistent and indicate that the source has mostly returned to its pre-event state.

new.title: Reconstructing the depth of first interaction in extensive air showers from fluorescence detector profiles with a physics-motivated neural network
new.summary: We present a physics-motivated neural network that reconstructs, event by event, the depth of the first interaction of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays from longitudinal profiles measured by fluorescence detectors. The network couples a convolutional encoder to a decoder that implements the Gaisser-Hillas function and predicts quantiles of the target, providing a per-event uncertainty estimate. It is trained and evaluated on four million proton- and iron-induced showers between $10^{18}$ and $10^{20}$ eV, simulated with the hadronic interaction models EPOS LHC-R and Sibyll 2.3d and processed by an end-to-end simulation of the fluorescence detector response. Despite detector effects, the reconstruction retains useful information for protons, achieving a mean absolute error of about 21 g$\,$cm$^{-2}$ for primary energies around $10^{19}$ eV, whereas for iron most of the information is lost. The reconstructed distributions preserve the exponential shape of the true ones, so the proton-air interaction length can be recovered from their tail with a model-related systematic uncertainty of approximately 4%. This value is limited mainly by the choice of the hadronic interaction model and is nearly insensitive to iron contamination. These results show that the depth of the first interaction can be reconstructed under realistic detection conditions, offering a complementary route to measurements of the proton-air cross section and mass-composition studies.

new.title: Archival X-Ray Observations of the Eclipsing Algol-type Binary TV~Cassiopeiae
new.summary: TV~Cassiopeiae (TV~Cas) is an eclipsing Algol-type binary with a B9\,V primary and an evolved late-type secondary in a 1.81-day orbit. We examine six serendipitous Chandra and two XMM-Newton observations spanning 2003--2012. The supplied Chandra spectra show thermal plasma near 1~keV and sub-solar fitted abundances, with an additional hotter component in one observation. EPIC-pn fits improve substantially with two temperatures: approximately 0.74/1.39~keV in 2003 and 0.87/2.16~keV in 2012. At 240~pc their nominal intrinsic 0.3--8~keV luminosities are $7.1\times10^{30}$ and $1.2\times10^{31}$~erg~s$^{-1}$, but residual structure, particularly in 2012, and response-calibration uncertainties limit physical interpretation. A prominent flare-like event occurs in Chandra ObsID 08458 (2006-11-04). The longest observation carried out in 2012 pn light curve spans approximately 82\% of an orbit and shows no conspicuous deep eclipse at the predicted secondary conjunction. An exploratory multi-epoch fold contains apparent troughs, but heterogeneous responses, intrinsic variability, and ephemeris uncertainty prevent a unique orbital interpretation. Thermal spectra and flare-like behavior favor a magnetically active secondary corona. The available products do not securely determine a coronal scale height, an orbital modulation amplitude, elemental abundance changes, or the fractional contributions of other unresolved emitters.

new.title: Constraining Gamma-Ray Emission Beyond the TOV Limit: A Targeted Fermi-GBM Search for Counterparts to 39 LVK Gravitational-Wave Candidates in GWTC-5.0
new.summary: We present a systematic search for sub-threshold gamma-ray counterparts within a one-day time window of 161 gravitational-wave (GW) events from the GWTC-5.0 catalog, whose inferred source masses exceed the adopted Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff (TOV) limit, using the Gamma-ray Targeted Search (GTS) pipeline. The search identifies 39 candidate GW--gamma-ray pairs satisfying the adopted joint likelihood-ratio thresholds. None of these candidates exhibits a temporal offset compatible with the prompt-emission delay observed for GW170817 ($\sim 1.7$ s); the smallest temporal separation is 17 min 17.976 s, ruling out GW170817-like prompt temporal associations in our candidate sample. Several candidates nevertheless show substantial spatial consistency. In particular, the most spatially consistent pair has a joint localization overlap of 95.4%, despite a temporal separation of 13 h 19 min 8.85 s, illustrating that high spatial agreement can occur by chance in the absence of temporal consistency. Among the sub-threshold gamma-ray candidates, we further identify an anomalous event with an exceptionally large single-instrument significance of log LR = 5250.84. For comparison, the adopted $3\sigma$ threshold corresponds to log LR $\approx 9$. The extreme likelihood ratio of this candidate motivates further investigation of trigger sensitivity, onboard veto configurations, and the statistical interpretation of sub-threshold events. Overall, we find no physically viable multi-messenger associations between the GWTC-5.0 events and the searched gamma-ray candidates, and derive corresponding upper limits on prompt high-energy emission from GWTC-5.0 progenitors.

new.title: Search for Axion-like Particles using Blazar Observations with the HAWC Observatory
new.summary: Axion-like particles (ALPs) can mix with photons in astrophysical magnetic fields, modifying the propagation of very-high-energy gamma rays from distant blazars and producing an energy-dependent enhancement of the observed flux relative to the standard expectation from absorption on the extragalactic background light (EBL). We search for this signature through a joint likelihood analysis of seven TeV BL Lac objects at redshifts $z = 0.14-0.60$, combining approximately 3,000 days of HAWC observations with published High Energy Spectroscopic System (H.E.S.S.), Major Atmospheric Gamma Imaging Cherenkov Telescopes (MAGIC), and Very Energetic Radiation Imaging Telescope Array System(VERITAS) spectra. We find no statistically significant ALP signal and derive exclusion limits using the $\mathrm{CL}_s$ method. We exclude photon-ALP couplings at the 95% $\mathrm{CL}_s$ level down to $5.5 \times 10^{-12}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$ for $m_a \lesssim 4$ neV and $4.6 \times 10^{-12}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$ near $m_a \approx 6-9$ neV. The systematic uncertainty on the excluded parameter-space area is $-36.5\%$ to $+32.6\%$, dominated by the choice of EBL model. Because the survival probability oscillates with the coupling, the excluded region is not simply connected, and we quote at each mass the lowest excluded coupling rather than an upper bound. The combined limit is set almost entirely by the highest-redshift detected source, PG 1553+113.

new.title: Radial and vertical structure of accretion discs around magnetized stars
new.summary: The ubiquity of accretion discs around magnetized stars motivates studies of the structure of these discs, in particular in whether the external magnetic field changes the radial and vertical profiles of pressure, temperature, and other quantities. We study the effects of the magnetic field of a central star on a steady accretion disc under the assumption that the magnetic field of the central star is able to partially penetrate the disc, with a degree of penetration quantified by a single parameter. We construct an analytical model of the interaction between the disc and the star's magnetic field. The equations of motion are modified to take the magnetic field into account. We solve the vertical structure of the disc assuming tabulated opacities and incorporate the magnetic field in order to determine the radial and vertical distributions of the disc parameters. The inner radius of the accretion disc, the viscous stress tensor, and the spin-up torque on the central object follow from the obtained distribution of the magnetic torque. In the limit where the stellar field is expelled from the disc, the inner radius scales with the Alfven radius, whereas when the external field penetrates the disc, the inner radius behaves in a more complex way, remaining within a few corotation radii. The normalized vertical profile depends only weakly on the radius and magnetic field. Nevertheless, the magnetic field can significantly modify the viscous stress tensor, radial structure, spectrum of the disc, and its thermal-equilibrium curves. The publicly available code AlphaDiSC now includes discs around magnetized stars.

new.title: Selection-aware inference of supernova kicks
new.summary: Observed compact objects (isolated or in binaries) used to infer natal kicks are selected by class membership, which depends on disruption, subsequent evolution, and discovery. Ignoring this selection can bias the inferred kicks. To demonstrate this bias in a comprehensive inference framework, we construct a differentiable model for key components of binary evolution, including correlated remnant-mass and kick prescriptions as well as survival probabilities. As initial conditions prior to the first SN, we use a fiducial COSMIC analysis. Using conventional statistical methods to assess bias due to omitted selection factors in a likelihood, we demonstrate this bias concretely. Reliable natal inference requires a forward prediction for both the observed properties and the probability of observing them. Our framework provides a novel method to enable robust neutron star population inference combining heterogeneous observations of multiple NS-pertinent observations.

new.title: The Sensitivity of Gamma-Ray Searches for Dark Matter Annihilation in Milky Way Dwarf Galaxies: the LSST Era and Beyond
new.summary: We forecast the sensitivity of gamma-ray searches to dark matter annihilation in Milky Way satellite dwarf galaxies using BabyBison, a Monte Carlo pipeline combining cosmological satellite simulations and observational selection functions with a joint likelihood analysis of gamma-ray data. Although LSST is expected to substantially expand the catalog of known satellite galaxies, we find that these discoveries are likely to produce only modest improvements in the resulting dark matter annihilation constraints, typically below 20\%. Much more substantial gains are possible, however, in relatively rare realizations that contain yet-to-be-discovered satellites with large $J$-factors. These results reinforce the fact that indirect detection analyses using the population of dwarf galaxies are typically driven in large part by a small number of high-$J$-factor systems rather than by the total satellite count. We present projections for the sensitivity of Fermi-LAT and the proposed Advanced Particle-astrophysics Telescope (APT) to dark matter annihilation, finding that a complete census of the Milky Way dwarf sample could enable such instruments to probe dark matter with masses up to the TeV scale. We also investigate the dark matter discovery potential of these instruments and project their ability to measure the properties of an annihilating dark matter particle.

new.title: The Gamma-ray Luminosity Function of Fermi BL Lacertae Objects
new.summary: We have used the largest sample of gamma-ray-selected Fermi BL Lacertae objects (1035 BL Lacs) ever used to determine the luminosity function and its evolution through cosmic time. This sample has its survey biases and selection effects well studied and a robust calculation of its detection efficiency. It spans a large range in luminosity ($L_{\gamma,min}$ = $5.71\times10^{40}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and $L_{\gamma,max}$ = $1.76\times10^{48}$ erg s$^{-1}$) and redshift ($ 0 < z \lesssim 4 $). We find that the local luminosity function follows a double power law. The density evolution of BL Lacs depends on the luminosity of the objects, with low-luminosity objects showing negative evolution (i.e., they are less common in the past) and high-luminosity objects showing positive evolution (i.e., they are more common in the past). We confirm that gamma-ray selected BL Lacs and FSRQs evolve similarly depending on their luminosities.

cross.title: Magnetic Reconnection and High-Speed Jets Downstream of a Parallel Shock: Full Particle-in-cell Simulations
cross.summary: Collisionless shocks are of fundamental interest in astrophysics and space physics as important sources of energetic particles. Downstream of quasi-parallel shocks, high-speed jets (HSJs) and magnetic reconnection have been frequently observed, while it remains unclear how their coupling shapes structured regions for particle energization. We use two-dimensional full particle-in-cell simulations to investigate HSJ generation, thin current sheet formation, and associated electron energization downstream of a parallel shock. We find that portions of foreshock ULF waves with enhanced dynamic pressure interact with a self-reforming shock front and are transmitted downstream, forming HSJs, while neighboring low pressure portions evolve into cavities. At the leading edge of the HSJs, the unique bent magnetic topology carried by the compressed ULF waves produces bow waves and locally squeezes out thin current sheets. These current sheets show reconnection signatures, including X-point topology, magnetic islands, enhanced $J\cdot E'$, and Alfvenic outflows along the local reconnecting direction. In the reconnection region associated with HSJs, the parallel electric field, betatron, and Fermi terms all contribute to adiabatic electron energization. The betatron term appears a visible signature near the X line, where the local magnetic structure is compressed by the HSJ. For the first time, we report a systematic mass-ratio dependence of HSJ morphology in full PIC simulations: lower mass ratios produce fragmented HSJs with shorter lifetimes, whereas larger mass ratios yield longer and wider HSJs with clearer bow waves as ion inertia increases.
